client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I keep trying to focus at work, but these memories of her just come out of nowhere and I can't get anything done. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help — it feels like nothing can really change the fact that she's gone.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief like this can feel completely overwhelming, and it makes sense that it's spilling into every part of your day. I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something in your voice that sounds almost quiet and exhausted, like maybe you're carrying more than the words themselves are letting on. I'm curious — beneath the doubt about whether talking will help, is there also a part of you that's just feeling really worn down, maybe even a little numb?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think that's actually pretty accurate — numb is a good word for it. It's like I go through the motions at work, I come home, I eat something, and then I just sit there staring at nothing, and I don't even feel sad in those moments, just... empty. And then out of nowhere something will trigger a memory — like I'll smell something that reminds me of her kitchen — and it all just crashes into me at once.
therapist: What you're describing — that flatness punctuated by these sudden waves of grief — is actually a really common and painful part of loss, and it makes complete sense given how much she meant to you. I'm noticing you're speaking quite quickly as you describe this, almost like the words are tumbling out, which makes me wonder if there's a lot stored up that hasn't had much space to be expressed yet. When those moments hit you — like the smell of her kitchen — what do you usually do with that feeling in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I just try to push it down and distract myself — I'll grab my phone, scroll through something mindless, anything to make it stop. I don't really let myself sit with it because when I do, it feels like it could just swallow me whole, like there's no bottom to it. I guess I'm scared that if I actually let myself feel it fully, I won't be able to function at all.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — it's actually a very natural protective response, your mind trying to keep you functional when the grief feels boundless. What's worth gently exploring, though, is that pushing it down often doesn't make the feeling smaller; it can actually build pressure, which might explain why it crashes in so hard when something catches you off guard. I'm wondering — has there ever been a time, even briefly, when you let yourself feel something difficult and found that it did eventually ease, rather than swallowing you whole?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean... maybe when my dog died a few years ago, I did let myself cry properly, like really cry, and eventually I fell asleep and woke up feeling a little lighter, not fine, but lighter. But this feels so much bigger than that — my grandmother was this constant presence in my life for 30 years, and I'm not sure the same thing applies. I guess I'm just not convinced that letting myself go there won't just make everything worse.
therapist: You actually just gave yourself some really important evidence there — that even in deep pain, you've experienced grief moving through you and leaving something a little lighter on the other side. It's true that losing your grandmother after 30 years is a much bigger loss, but I'm curious whether the size of the love might also mean the grief deserves even more room to be felt, rather than less. What do you think she would have wanted for you in how you carry this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, because I know exactly what she would have said — she was always telling me not to bottle things up, that feelings need somewhere to go. But knowing that and actually doing it feel like completely different things, and there's this guilt on top of it all, like I should be handling this better, like I'm somehow letting her down by falling apart. I think part of me feels like if I grieve too openly, it's admitting she's really gone, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that.
therapist: What you just shared is so tender and important — the guilt of "not handling it well enough" is actually one of grief's cruelest tricks, turning your love for her into a reason to judge yourself. And that last part, about grieving meaning admitting she's really gone — that's not weakness or falling apart, that's one of the hardest truths a person can face. I wonder if, rather than letting her down, allowing yourself to grieve might actually be one of the most faithful ways of honoring how real and irreplaceable she was to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe actually hits me somewhere deep, and I wasn't expecting it to. Like, I've been so focused on the idea that grieving means losing her all over again, but maybe it's actually the opposite — maybe it's the way I keep her real. I still don't fully know how to do that though, because every time I try to sit with it, I feel so alone in it, like there's no one around me who really gets how much she meant to me.
therapist: That shift you just made — from "grieving means losing her" to "grieving keeps her real" — is genuinely profound, and it sounds like something in you recognized its truth immediately. The loneliness you're describing, feeling like no one around you truly understands the scale of this loss, can make grief so much heavier to carry. I'm wondering, is there anyone in your life who knew her well, someone who might actually share that depth of feeling and could perhaps grieve alongside you rather than you having to hold this alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: My mom knew her just as well as I did, and I know she's grieving too, but we've both just been sort of... tiptoeing around it with each other, like we're both trying to protect the other one from feeling worse. I've thought about bringing it up with her, but I'm scared it'll just turn into both of us falling apart at the same time and neither of us being able to hold it together. I guess I don't really trust that sharing it would bring us closer — it feels just as likely that it could make things more painful.
therapist: It's really touching that you and your mom are both trying to protect each other — that itself is a form of love, even if it's keeping you both isolated in your grief. I notice as you talk about her, your voice becomes quite soft, almost careful, like even describing this feels delicate — and I wonder if what feels like a risk of "both falling apart" might actually be two people finally feeling seen in the same loss. What if falling apart together, even for a moment, is exactly what allows you both to hold each other rather than hold it in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe that, but I also know my mom — she tends to shut down when things get too emotional, and I worry that if I open that door and she closes it on me, I'll feel even more alone than I do now. It's like the risk of reaching out and being met with silence or deflection feels worse than just staying in this quiet, separate grief we're both doing. I don't know how I'd even start that conversation without it feeling forced or like I'm putting something heavy on her.
therapist: The fear of reaching out and being met with silence is so understandable — rejection in a moment of vulnerability can feel devastating, especially when you're already hurting. What strikes me is that you're essentially facing the same dilemma your mom probably is too, both of you wanting connection but scared of getting it wrong. I'm wondering if the conversation doesn't have to start with the heaviest thing — is there a smaller, gentler way in, like simply telling her you've been missing your grandmother and asking how she's been holding up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That does feel more manageable than launching into some big emotional conversation, and I can see the logic in it. But I guess my worry is that even a small opening like that could unravel quickly, and I'm not sure I'd be able to keep it light if she actually said she was struggling too — I think I'd just start crying and then feel embarrassed about it. I'm not great at being vulnerable in front of my mom specifically, there's a lot of history there around being "the strong one" in the family.
therapist: There's something interesting I'm noticing — the words you're using are careful and a little hesitant, but there's an energy in your voice right now that sounds almost animated, like this topic is alive in a way that feels significant. I wonder if underneath the worry about crying or losing control, there's actually a part of you that really *wants* to be seen by your mom, that's maybe even a little excited by the possibility, even if it also feels terrifying. And I'm curious about this role of "the strong one" — who decided that was your job, and has carrying it ever actually felt like a choice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, no, it never really felt like a choice — it was just something that happened gradually, like I was the one who kept it together when things got hard and eventually everyone just expected that from me, including myself. And you're right that there's a part of me that desperately wants my mom to just see me as someone who's hurting right now, not the person who holds everyone else up. But admitting that even to you feels uncomfortable, like I'm betraying some version of myself I've been for so long that I don't know who I am without it.
therapist: What you just said — not knowing who you are without the "strong one" role — that's such a courageous and important thing to recognize, and it makes complete sense that it feels uncomfortable, because you're touching something that goes much deeper than grief. It sounds like your grandmother's death hasn't just brought loss of her, but is also stirring up a bigger question about whether you're allowed to need things, to be held, to be human in front of the people you love. I'm wondering — what would it mean for you, not for anyone else, just for you, if you let yourself be the one who's hurting for a little while?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
